notes.meaning: A huge crowd has gathered, so packed that people are stepping on each other. Jesus speaks first to His own disciples and tells them, above all, to watch out for hypocrisy, which means pretending to be more godly than you really are. He calls it 'leaven,' or yeast, because a little of it quietly spreads through the whole person and puffs them up with pride. Even His closest followers needed this warning, because they were to teach others.

Pretending is pointless, because the truth always comes out in the end. What is hidden behind a show of faith will be shown, sometimes in this life and surely on the day God judges every heart. Back then, news was shouted from flat rooftops so everyone could hear. Some also read these verses as a call to preach openly what Jesus taught them in private.

Jesus tenderly calls His disciples 'friends' as He warns them that following Him may cost their lives. People can only kill the body, and even that only as far as God allows. God alone has power over what happens after death, so He is the one to fear, with deep respect. When we fear God rightly, the fear of people loses its grip on us.

Sparrows were so cheap that buying a few more pennies' worth got you an extra one thrown in. Yet God does not forget even one of them. He knows you so closely that He has counted the hairs on your head. You are worth far more to Him than birds, so you can trust Him and not be afraid.

To 'confess' Jesus means to openly own Him as your Lord, even when it brings shame or danger. Those who do will be owned by Him before God's angels on the last day. Those who turn their backs on Him to save themselves will be disowned. Whatever they gain by it, they lose far more in the end.

Even someone who has spoken against Jesus can be forgiven if they truly repent. That is a great comfort to anyone who has failed Him. 'Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit' is something different: a settled, hard-hearted hatred of God's work, like calling the Spirit's good works evil. It will never be forgiven because the person never turns back in repentance.

Jesus' followers would be dragged before religious courts and rulers. He tells them not to panic about how to defend themselves. The Holy Spirit will give them the right words at the right moment, as He later did for Peter and John in Acts 4. This is a promise of courage in a crisis, not an excuse to skip preparing.

A man in the crowd interrupts Jesus' serious teaching with a family money fight. The law gave the older brother a double share of the estate. The man does not ask Jesus to hear both sides; he wants Jesus to take his side. Some think his brother had truly cheated him, but Jesus' reply suggests greed was at the root.

Jesus refuses to act as a judge over the inheritance. Notice He calls the man simply 'Man,' not 'friend.' His kingdom is spiritual, not a worldly government, and He did not come to settle property cases; that belongs to courts and officials. This does not mean Christians can never serve as judges. It means each person should stay within the calling God has given.

Jesus turns the moment into a warning for everyone: guard yourselves against every kind of greed, the hunger to always have more. Your life is not made up of how much you own. Wealth cannot make your soul happy, and it cannot add a single day to your life, which rests in God's hands.

Jesus tells a story about a rich man whose land gave a huge harvest. A good harvest is a blessing from God. But God often gives such blessings even to people who do not honor Him, so wealth is no sign of God's approval.

Instead of thanking God or thinking how to help others, the man worries: 'What shall I do?' A starving beggar could hardly sound more anxious. Riches often bring more worry, not less. God also hears the thoughts we 'only think to ourselves.'

His plan is to tear down his barns and build bigger ones to hold everything. Notice how he keeps saying 'my' crops and 'my' goods, as if they were not God's on loan. He plans to keep it all for himself, with no thought of the poor and no 'if the Lord wills.' Storing grain is not wrong; his endless greed is.

He tells his own soul to relax and enjoy many years of eating, drinking and fun. He thinks food and goods can satisfy his soul, which was made for God. He also assumes he has many years left. This is the outlook of someone living only for this life.

Everyone would have called him a success, but God calls him a fool. That very night his life will be demanded from him, and he must give account to God. All he stored up stays behind, and he cannot know who will end up with it. His life was never in his own control.

Jesus says this is how it goes for anyone who piles up wealth for himself but is not 'rich toward God.' Being rich toward God means trusting Him rather than possessions, and being rich in faith, love and good works. The story does not condemn money itself, but a life lived with no thought of God or eternity.

Now Jesus speaks to His disciples, who had little money. Their danger was not pride in riches but worry about having enough. He tells them not to fret over food and clothes. God already gave them life and a body, the bigger gifts, so they can trust Him for the smaller things.
Ravens do not plant crops or keep barns, unlike the rich man, yet God feeds them. You matter far more to God than birds do. Much of our worry comes from forgetting how much God values us.

Worry cannot add even an hour to your life, which is a very small thing. If you cannot do even that, why worry about everything else? Worry changes nothing, so it is wise to accept what we cannot change and trust it to God's care.

Wildflowers do no work and make no clothes, yet God dresses them more beautifully than King Solomon in all his splendor. They bloom for a day and are then burned as fuel. If God takes such care of them, He will surely clothe His children. Our worry shows how small our faith is.

Jesus tells His disciples not to chase after food and drink or live tossed up and down by anxious thoughts. People who do not know God make these things their whole life. But believers have a Father in heaven who already knows what they need. Instead of worrying, they can ask Him daily and trust His care.
